title: Time to focus on cost of living, says PM after US election results
description: Andy Burnham has said the results of the US midterm elections meant there was an "opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all,
body: Andy Burnham has said the results of the US midterm elections meant there was an "opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living".Speaking to broadcasters from the Commonwealth leaders summit, the prime minister promised to push for a resolution to the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine in the wake of the US elections that saw Donald Trump's Republicans suffer heavy losses.He said he couldn't ease cost of living pressures until the US's conflict in Iran had been resolved.Responding to the midterm results, the US president acknowledged that rising fuel prices - caused by the Iran war - had played a part in his party's defeats.Speaking to Fox News, President Trump said: "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that."Giving his reaction to the results, Burnham said the voters in the US have said they want to "see the world coming together and focusing on the things that matter to people".Asked whether he thought the results might make the US president more unpredictable, Burnham said: "President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living."That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we've made moves."But I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia. "These are the things we have to focus on now, and I hope the world has a moment to do that."And certainly, in my calls with leaders, that is what I will be asking everybody to do."The subject of the US midterm elections was raised at Prime Minister's Questions, which, in Burnham's absence, was taken by Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh. The Liberal Democrat's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said American voters had rejected Trump's "warmongering and the economic chaos that it has caused".She expressed concern that the US president was planning further strikes on Iran and urged the government to "stand together with our reliable allies and send a clear message to Trump and Netanyahu: there must be no more strikes."Haigh replied: "The US are one of our most important allies and our priority absolutely is de-escalation."She said the Iran war had been "catastrophic for the cost of living crisis" and said the Conservatives and Reform should "consider very carefully their judgment in calling for us to jump so readily into it".Asked about suggestions there could be an attack on Iran in the coming week, Trump told the Financial Times, external on Tuesday: "The US was "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".Indirect talks between the two sides have been stalled for months and some analysts close to the Iran regime have suggested prolonging the negotiations, in the hope that the rising cost of fuel would damage Trump electorally.  Although the US Congress, now controlled by the Democrats, can restrict funding, Trump will still have significant authority over foreign policy.Burnham is preparing a 10-year plan for government, and will be hoping that his strategy isn't blown off course by the actions of an unpredictable US president in his last two years in the White House.

schema.headline: Time to focus on cost of living, says PM after US election results

title: Miliband says slavery apology will not bring cost for UK taxpayers
description: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has insisted the government's willingness to consider formally apologising for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave
body: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has insisted the government's willingness to consider formally apologising for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave trade will not lead to higher costs for the British taxpayer.The prime minister has said the UK will not pay reparations to affected countries, but declined to say whether his new approach could involve additional taxpayer money.Speaking on the BBC's Newscast podcast, Miliband said previous British governments had a "sweep it under the carpet" attitude to the pain and consequences of slavery, citing what he described as former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair's "sorry not sorry" remarks on the issue nearly two decades ago.In 2007, Sir Tony said the UK's involvement in the slave trade was a matter of "deep sorrow and regret"."Tony Blair did sort of do a kind of sorry not sorry situation. He kind of expressed sorrow, and then said sorry, and then it was walked back by number 10," Miliband said.Miliband said the former prime minister's approach was still referred to and came up in a recent conversation between Andy Burnham and the Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Mottley.In addition, Miliband claimed, he and Burnham inherited a more recent mess, which is how the last Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) played out in Samoa two years ago.Miliband said: "On the second day as my time as foreign secretary, I was told, 'look, one of your tasks is CHOGM 2024, which happened in Samoa, didn't go well.' To use sort of diplomatic speak, it ended up in a sort of punch up, a sort of verbal punch up about this whole issue." He added: "This has really been hanging around as an issue for the Commonwealth for sort of 20 years, really. But it's grown and grown."Given that, Miliband said, "we thought it was right to confront this issue and not to just try and sort of pretend that it didn't exist".Burnham now says the government is open to formally apologising for slavery. Ministers are beginning what they call a "structured dialogue" with affected countries, with the expectation that the apology may come at around the time the prime minister hosts the G20 Summit of world leaders in Manchester in November 2027."Is it weak to do this? I think it's the opposite of weak. I think fragile weak countries can't face up to their past. I'm really proud of Britain, but being proud of your country is also being willing to face up to things you didn't do, right?" Miliband said.He said he had asked to be provided with a historical digest of the UK's involvement in the slave trade."Over three million people shipped, really with the British state's complicity, over a long period of time, couple of centuries actually, hundreds of thousands of them didn't make it and died," the foreign secretary said."Those who did make it had appalling conditions. Reading about the conditions on the ships and what happened to them when they arrived in the Caribbean and the Americas is really pretty harrowing."Now he and the prime minister begin a process likely to formally apologise for this -and, they hope, create space for the Commonwealth to turn its attention to other things.

schema.headline: Miliband says slavery apology will not bring cost for UK taxpayers

title: Israel's president to begin consultations with parties after election deadlock
description: In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knes
body: In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.That makes them potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.The role of Israel's president is largely ceremonial, but after an election they have the role of inviting a Knesset member to form a government. That person will be given 28 days to do so, with a potential 14-day extension.The president has wide discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition. They do not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.On Wednesday morning, Herzog was presented with the official results by Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg at a ceremony in Jerusalem."In recent days, we have heard voices trying to cast doubt on the election results and to undermine their legitimacy. This is a real danger," Sohlberg said."One of the foundations of democracy is the ability to have a peaceful transfer of power. This stems from the understanding that the will of the electorate obligates us all."Herzog announced that he would begin the consultation process on Wednesday evening."In order to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable and good government here for the people of Israel, I expect the factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled," he said.The president also expressed confidence in the Shin Bet's ability to investigate the allegations of foreign interference in the election and appealed for patience.But he warned that Arab Israelis - who make up about one fifth of the population and often refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel - "must not be smeared"."I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently. There is no place for them toward any community in Israel," he said.Earlier, Sohlberg told a meeting of the Central Elections Committee that the Shin Bet's intelligence appeared to point to a "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states", some of which were hostile.It believed further investigation was needed to "connect the dots and determine the scale of the phenomenon with a high degree of certainty", he said.Last week, Israeli media reported that the committee had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's foreign ministry said it categorically denied the allegation.Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party and an ally of the prime minister, called on the Shin Bet to arrest all the leaders of Arab parties and interrogate them "until these suspicions are fully clarified".Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen accused Ben-Gvir and the prime minister of attempting to "steal the election from the public".On Tuesday, Eisenkot alleged that Netanyahu and his Likud party were "trying to carry out a veritable pogrom against democracy and the rule of law".His comments came after Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected a reported demand by Shin Bet chief David Zini - an appointee of the prime minister - to interrogate four Arab politicians, saying no evidence of wrongdoing had been presented.Likud accused Baharav-Miara of trying to "obstruct the investigation and to cover up this serious case of manipulation of the electoral process by foreign actors".

schema.headline: Israel's president to begin consultations with parties after election deadlock

title: Children spending too long on maths app TT Rockstars, MP warns
description: Concerns have been raised with the government about the amount of time primary school children are spending on a game designed to make learning times
body: Concerns have been raised with the government about the amount of time primary school children are spending on a game designed to make learning times tables fun.TT Rockstars, which allows children to compete with their classmates for virtual coins and rock-star themed characters and outfits, is widely used by schools for maths homework.Labour MP Emily Darlington said the app and others like it could be harming children's development because it rewards them for "length of time rather than quality of time spent online".Bruno Reddy, founder of the firm behind TT Rockstars, said he shared concerns about screen time and was working with schools to bring in curfews and time limits.He said the company discourages long sessions, adding: "Every game in TTRS is deliberately short, and our characters remind children to take regular breaks."The rule of thumb we give schools is: three minutes, four or five times a week. In September, a typical child played on three days, for about six minutes each time."He said that from 24 November "every school will have a curfew and a daily time limit switched on, and leaderboards switched off as default".Darlington told BBC News that while education technology, or EdTech, can have a place in the classroom "when gamification is used, children spend hours online to 'earn' the latest outfit". "Parents are concerned that this causes conflict on time spent on devices and the pressure to perform against classmates," she added, and this could deter them from taking part in real life, rather than screen-based, activities. The Milton Keynes Central MP raised concerns about TT Rockstars on Tuesday at the Commons Science Committee, which is investigating the impact of screen time and digital devices on children's brain development.The company behind TT Rockstars, Maths Circle, says that the app and a similar programme for addition and subtraction, Numbots, is used in 17,000 schools and over 100,000 households.Reddy, a former maths teacher, said TT Rockstars had been designed to "boost learning in the classroom: recognising progress, celebrating achievement and making learning enjoyable".He added: "We've deliberately steered away from features designed to keep children playing, such as streaks, random rewards, chat messages, loot boxes or notifications."There's no advertising and schools pay the same subscription however much their students play, so we have no commercial reason to want children on screen for longer."The government is in the process of drawing up guidelines for schools and parents on the amount of time five to 16-year-olds should spend on screens.At the committee, early years education minister Paul Waugh said: "Gamification isn't the way to learn."That's the propaganda they [EdTech companies] will give you but it is all about driving their screen time and their screen use. So it's profit driven."He said there were "ways of making learning fun" that did not involve "competition with yourself or with someone else" and EdTech should be about supporting teachers and not replacing them.It comes amid growing calls for the use of EdTech in the classroom to be limited.Charlotte Ashton, co-founder of Generation Focus, which campaigns for smartphone-free schools, said: "Increasingly parents and teachers are saying no to Ed Tech because for the vast majority of digital 'learning tools' there's very little evidence they actually improve learning and growing evidence they can be harmful."She added:  "Not all tech is bad, but until we are confident that new digital tools improve children's learning without doing harm or imposing unintended consequences we are supporting schools to stick to proven teaching methods."

schema.headline: Children spending too long on maths app TT Rockstars, MP warns

title: All's Fair: Why Kim Kardashian came back to 'the worst TV drama ever'
description: "We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is the
body: "We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is they can see what the response is and write accordingly to that."All's Fair, which was created by American Horror Story and Glee showrunner Ryan Murphy, became the Hulu network's most-watched scripted series debut of the last three years and was immediately renewed.Following a group of divorce lawyers - played by Kardashian, Close, Paulson, Naomi Watts and Niecy Nash-Betts - the show was panned for bad acting, with Kardashian bearing the brunt of criticism.The Hollywood Reporter called her "wooden", and the Times declared that the show "may be the worst TV drama ever".But the hallmark of Kardashian's career has been her ability to back herself - whether that's going from years of being snubbed by Met Gala organisers to becoming its most anticipated guest, or overcoming backlash to the launch of her shapewear company to turn it into a $5bn (£3.7bn) brand.Kardashian says: "What is the alternative, right? What is the other choice that you have when you're getting criticised?"Do you just fall in and feel that, or keep your head down and try better, try harder and try a different path?"Having been in the spotlight for more than 20 years, she's "always had a really good sense of my mental health", and says that comes from being able to "brush off" those who seek to bring her down."I always do things that are tough because I genuinely want to learn," Kardashian says.While she was promoting the legal drama last year, Kardashian was waiting to find out if she had passed exams to become a lawyer in real life, after six years of studying for an apprenticeship that negated the need for a university degree.Shortly after the first series aired, she found out she had failed the exam - but says that won't be the end of her pursuit of the qualification."If I don't pass something, if I don't do the best at something, then I'll get there," she says. "I don't worry. I just have to keep going."But after her admission that she had used AI for legal advice, external, she does say she will change how public she is about her studies."I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there," says Kardashian, who has four children with rapper Kanye West and is now in a relationship with British Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton. "I know there was a lot of talk out there like, 'she's given up', and that's funny to me. "I like people to think what they want to think and I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," she says.Audiences have only been given a glimpse of what to expect from the second series of All's Fair so far.Co-star Watts, who also serves as a producer on the show alongside Kardashian, says they have "doubled down" on "the high fashion, high drama and heightened reality" that audiences enjoyed the first time around.As for Kardashian's acting, Watts says she's on a "trajectory" that sees her "stepping up in the second season"."She was improvising, riffing, doing all kind of things that I thought were deeply impressive," Watts adds, to which Kardashian jokes: "I think I'm just naturally so funny."One of the positives that critics did cite was the show's desire to spotlight the duality of professional women who were both feminine and successful, which Kardashian says she "loves" because it is "a really realistic depiction of a lot of women I know"."It doesn't mean that just because you're super smart that you can't be fashionable and into glamorous things as well," she adds.

schema.headline: All's Fair: Why Kim Kardashian came back to 'the worst TV drama ever'

title: JJ Gabriel: Real Madrid confident of signing Manchester United forward
description: Real Madrid are confident of winning the race to sign Manchester United forward JJ Gabriel after reaching a verbal agreement with the teenager. The 16
body: Real Madrid are confident of winning the race to sign Manchester United forward JJ Gabriel after reaching a verbal agreement with the teenager. The 16-year-old is registered at United, but has not been back to the club since walking out in September.Gabriel, who played against Atletico Madrid on United's pre-season tour, had been expected to become the club's youngest debutant in September's Carabao Cup tie against Brighton.However, he has opted to look elsewhere for senior football and has been training on his own in Spain.His availability alerted clubs around Europe, including Barcelona and Paris St-Germain, but Real now expect to sign the youngster in January.Though no club-to-club talks have been held, sources have told BBC Sport Real have verbally agreed a deal with Gabriel and his representatives. Gabriel, who scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut, has secured a European Union passport, which is expected to make it easier for him to sign for a club outside England.United would be due compensation should Gabriel leave, although the figure will be lower if he signs for a club outside the Premier League.He was named the Premier League's Under-18 player of the season last term, despite being only 14 when the season campaign."The best 15-year-old in Europe," was how Gabriel was described by a United source this year, while former interim manager Darren Fletcher said: "The world is his oyster."Speaking after the EFL Cup defeat by Brighton, United head coach Michael Carrick said: "We've got to be really careful of the whole situation."He's a young boy...from a club point of view, looking after our younger players - their welfare, their well-being, their exposure - we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation."

schema.headline: JJ Gabriel: Real Madrid confident of signing Manchester United forward

title: Kellogg's admits snap, crackle and pop is quieter after uproar over Rice Krispies recipe change
description: Kellogg's has told the BBC the "snap, crackle and pop" sound made by its Rice Krispies may be noticeably quieter after an uproar over the cereal giant
body: Kellogg's has told the BBC the "snap, crackle and pop" sound made by its Rice Krispies may be noticeably quieter after an uproar over the cereal giant's recipe change. Rice Krispies and Coco Pops are no longer being made with whole rice grains, with the tiny toasted puffs being made using corn flour and rice flour instead.A Kellogg's spokesperson said retaining the iconic sound had been a "huge focus" when designing the new recipe, but that customers "might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before". The firm was responding to complaints online that the taste of the breakfast staples had changed, with some fans adding they missed the "pop" sound.Kellogg's said it had adapted the recipes due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies of some grains and cereals.The cereal giant said the new versions had been "carefully assessed for taste, appearance and texture", but some shoppers said their children would no longer eat them.Some expressed dismay that the taste and texture were "totally different" and dubbed the change "grim" and "disgusting". "There's no snap, crackle and pop in these," a parent named Dani wrote on TikTok. "My toddler won't eat them."Lauren, also posting on TikTok, added that she had been eating Rice Krispies every day for breakfast "for years and years"."I had a bowl of the new recipe and you can immediately tell the difference," she said. "They don't have the snapping sound when you put in the milk."Jessicake meanwhile said they tasted "weird and stale".The "Snap, Crackle and Pop" - made when milk is added to the puffed rice - has been a centrepiece of the brand's marketing since the 1950s.Kellogg's insisted the snap, crackle and pop is "still there, but consumers might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before".Recipe changes are notoriously difficult for big brands. Chocolate makers are constantly accused of reducing cocoa content in their products and debates rage online over whether ketchup ingredients have changed. When Scottish fizzy drink Irn Bru cut its sugar content in 2018, fans famously stockpiled crates of the old version.No changes are being made to Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada.Kellogg's said the recipe change in the UK would help "maintain consistent quality" as extreme weather takes a toll on crops and pushes up ingredient prices.Extreme weather in Spain in 2022 and 2023 in particular had reduced availability of the types of rice the company uses for its breakfast cereals, the company saidRice Krispies, launched nearly a century ago, are sold around the world and come in variations such as vanilla and strawberry flavours in some markets alongside the widespread chocolate-flavoured Coco Pops version."We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration," Kellogg's said.The firm said it appreciated the customer feedback and would "continue to look at ways to make [its] products even better in the future".The cereals have already undergone some change, with reductions in salt content in the 1990s and lowered sugar in 2018. The company said Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food.A backlash against processed foods in recent years, especially those low in fibre and high in sugar, has put cereals generally under the spotlight from healthy eating advocates.Kellogg's stressed the cereals contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same.However, the new recipes mean packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning.Previously packaging said the products "may contain gluten" because they were made in a factory handling other cereals and there was a risk of cross-contamination. Kellogg's said it has not changed the recipe for any of its other cereals.Many parts of the world have been affected by droughts, floods and heatwaves this year due to the El Niño weather phenomenon. The weather event is expected to severely affect crop production from South East Asia in particular. The region produces more than a quarter of the world's rice.The World Meteorological Agency expects the record-breaking El Niño will last until at least 2027.That will intensify pressure on food manufacturing companies, already looking at ways to source reliable and affordable ingredients.The original Kellogg company separated into two distinct firms in 2023. The largest is Kellanova, which focuses on snacks, cereals, noodles and other food products like Eggo, Pringles and Pop-Tarts sold globally. It is now owned by Mars, which makes confectionery and pet food.The other business, WK Kellogg's, operates in North America and has since been taken over by Italian chocolate giant Ferrero.

schema.headline: Kellogg's admits snap, crackle and pop is quieter after uproar over Rice Krispies recipe change

title: Jesus de Miguel death: Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono 'would never intentionally hurt anyone' says team-mate
description: Figure caption, Fans pay respects to Tenerife's De MiguelByDavid WatkinsonBBC Sport senior journalistGoalkeeper Jesus Owono "would never intentionally
body: Figure caption, Fans pay respects to Tenerife's De MiguelByDavid WatkinsonBBC Sport senior journalistGoalkeeper Jesus Owono "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and has been "deeply affected" by the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel, an FC Andorra team-mate said on Wednesday.Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday.The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all European games this week.Writing on social media, FC Andorra centre-back Lautaro Spatz said Owono was devastated.He paid tribute to De Miguel but added: "I also want to say a few words about my team-mate, goalkeeper and friend, who is deeply affected by what has happened."Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone."In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."Players from Andorra held a minute's silence before a voluntary training session on Wednesday. Owono did not attend the session.Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.The 25-year-old goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.The president of Equatorial Guinea's football federation, Venancio Tomas Micha, issued a statement on Tuesday offering "all our human and professional backing" to the player."As the involuntary protagonist of this tragic incident in the game, he is living through this situation with deep sorrow and distress," he added.Image source, AlamyImage caption, Jesus de Miguel joined Tenerife in 2025 on a three-year dealPeriod of mourningOn Tuesday, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.Tenerife said in a statement they will commence six official days of mourning, with all club activities suspended during this time.The club's players, staff and officials will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, Toledo.Tenerife will also open their home ground on Saturday evening to allow supporters to "bid a fitting farewell"."Jesus de Miguel's family would like to thank everyone for their messages of support and, from the bottom of their hearts, ask that their privacy be respected at this terrible time. May he rest in peace," added the club statement.Tenerife and Andorra's Spanish second division matches scheduled for the weekend, against Granada and Mallorca respectively, have been postponed.

schema.headline: Jesus de Miguel death: Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono 'would never intentionally hurt anyone' says team-mate

title: Graduates jobs: More work with AI but what else?
description: Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.Underwo
body: Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing.She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation.A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media.Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others."A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood.What is an AI agent?AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts, but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's.Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement.Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI."My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel.Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company.CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI."We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell."We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way."Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role."If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier.Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires.For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, external, it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building.Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%.There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers.But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?Underwood says she'd like to still pick up the traditional PR skills her role isn't currently focused on, but is confident of her future in the agency's growing AI team."There's certain things that I haven't had the chance to do yet, like directly pitching to the media. I absolutely plan to do this," she says.Graduates becoming too AI-centric is an issue for Simon Pratt, chief operating officer at Portman Finance Group. He says being able to use AI effectively is important, but the company's two-year graduate programme is fully centred on "learning the trade"."Our graduates rotate across four areas at six-month intervals, working directly alongside senior relationship managers to learn their trade," Northampton-based Pratt explains."They'll learn all of our financial products, how to draft credit papers for submission to lenders, and how to build meaningful relationships with our customers. They'll progress to running transactions from start to finish."Claire Reid, PwC UK's chief technology and innovation officer, believes graduate roles that are too AI heavy won't necessarily provide graduates long-term career progression."There will be no graduate job now that doesn't require a baseline of AI literacy," says Glasgow-based Reid."But AI skills on their own are not going to help you in your career. You've got to couple that with that sector knowledge of what that client actually wants."Back in Coventry, Dillan Patel is confident his AI work will continue to be valuable, and he wants to keep building on it."I don't think I'd want to explore different positions within the business. Through my involvement in AI-related projects, I already work closely with different areas of the business and I'm gaining valuable knowledge and experience along the way," he says.

schema.headline: Graduates jobs: More work with AI but what else?

title: Code cracked for Margam shipwreck padlock solving 400-year-old mystery
description: Image source, Amgueddfa CymruImage caption, The brass lock was discovered off the Welsh coast and dates back to 1583ByMeleri WilliamsBBC WalesUpdated
body: Image source, Amgueddfa CymruImage caption, The brass lock was discovered off the Welsh coast and dates back to 1583ByMeleri WilliamsBBC WalesUpdated 9 hours agoExperts have cracked a four-letter code to open an ancient padlock from a shipwreck off the Welsh coast using modern scanning technology.The 400-year-old brass lock was discovered by metal detectorist Peter Hughes in the sand near Margam in Port Talbot, in 1999.It forms part of a wider treasure hoard from the Ann Francis ship that was caught in a storm on 28 December 1583 on the way back from Spain. Its cargo was hidden beneath the sand for centuries.Museum experts have used CT scanning to examine the lock's internal mechanism, identify the correct letter combination and solve the mystery.Image caption, Peter Hughes found the lock, along with coins and other artefacts, while walking with his metal detectorPeter Hughes, from Maesteg, said the padlock was one of hundreds of artefacts he found after decades of searching on Morfa beach.Found near a collection of Spanish silver coins and close to two coin weights, it is thought the lock may have protected these objects or secured a chest containing valuable items that did not survive, like documents or textiles."It was by chance - a day off. I was walking along the beach with my metal detector on a day off, and I came across a coin," the 69-year-old said."That was the start of a journey that lasted 21 years."Image caption, The code spells out ANCE and the inside resembles a keyHe said he was "delighted" that the expert team at Amgueddfa Cymru and Cardiff University cracked the padlock code after he spent years trying to solve the mystery himself."I tried to unlock it for about 20 years, I tried moving the dials, finding the right combinations, and I failed," he said."But with the aid of modern technology we've been able to crack what's like the Da Vinci code, really."For me, it's like opening the Ark of the Covenant, and I'm delighted, truly thrilled."'Cracking the code was like a puzzle'Dr David Williams, a research associate based at Cardiff University's School of Engineering, said he was "sceptical" when he was asked to use a scanning device to try and solve the mystery."It's challenging, the device we have is not designed to this particular purpose," he said."This is micro CT scanning, something you'd get at the hospital, but for smaller items."Williams said he was "always open to a challenge" and trying to "figure out a puzzle"."We did a first scan to see if we could see anything and we were quite surprised that we could see letters," he said."The second scan went terribly, but with the third scan, we tried a different approach, and figured out the code."I was blown away that we actually cracked it."Image caption, Senior curator Alastair Willis said the unlocking was complexHughes passed on the hoard of artefacts to Amgueddfa Cymru in 2017, and the collection, with the lock in the centre, was put on display at Swansea Waterfront Museum in July 2026.Senior curator Alastair Willis said the discovery of the code, which spells out ANCE, was "incredible"."It's really complex because there are so many combinations," he said."There are four different rings, and because there are six different letters on each of the rings, there are 1,296 different combinations, and you have to make sure they're aligned with the loop at the top.""Also, confusingly, there are other letters on the ends which don't move, which are unrelated, and it's like they were to mislead any potential burglar," he added.Image caption, Siân Iles works as a senior curator with Amgueddfa Cymru and said the team were "intrigued" with the brass lockHis colleague at Amgueddfa Cymru, senior curator Siân Iles, said the lock was in "excellent condition" and paints a picture of the period."This is a wonderful example of one that still functions as it would have done hundreds of years ago," she said."Because it was found so close to the wreck of the Ann Francis and with all the material that's part of that collection, it provides a really good context, it allows us to really tightly date it."I've seen others, and they're usually corroded and in different parts, but it was in wonderful condition."It's a small object so it probably would have been a lock for a chest or a small box, we don't know the content, and that's part of the story, there are some things we'll never know, but it's something that would have meant something to the person who knew that code."What should you do if you discover treasure?Treasure has a variety of definitions, external, as per the Treasure Act of 1996.In Wales, if you find treasure it must be reported to a Finds Liaison Officer, external within 14 days of first finding it or within 14 days of realising an item might be treasure, even if you have had it for longer.Only items officially defined as treasure need to be reported and there is a fine or up to three months in prison for not reporting.There are different rules for Scotland, external and Northern Ireland, external.After a find is reported, you will be contacted by either a Finds Liaison Officer or museum curator to talk about how and where you made the find. The Finds Liaison Officer or museum curator will then write a report on the find and the coroner will hold an inquest. The Finds Liaison Officer will help you get the coins assessed by experts to determine if they meet the legal definition of "treasure" under the Treasure Act 1996, external.If a museum wants the treasure, the Treasure Valuation Committee will ask an expert to value the find.They will recommend to the Secretary of State for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, external how much the treasure is worth and how much should go to anyone eligible for a share of a reward.

schema.headline: Code cracked for Margam shipwreck padlock solving 400-year-old mystery

title: Could Hyrox's Olympic ambition spell the end for triathlon?
description: "Our biggest concern is that they're not just here to take part, they're here to take over."British triathlete Max Stapley first saw the news on Insta
body: "Our biggest concern is that they're not just here to take part, they're here to take over."British triathlete Max Stapley first saw the news on Instagram. Last week, World Triathlon announced it was partnering with Hyrox - the fitness craze which combines running with exercise stations.The agreement means Hyrox becomes a recognised discipline within World Triathlon. And now it sits under a recognised international federation, it could be eligible for inclusion at the Olympics and Paralympics.It is too late for the Los Angeles 2028 Games but is there room for both hybrid racing and triathlon to feature at a future Olympics? Or could one replace the other?For triathlon, a sport which has been in the Olympics since 2000, and has long-established professional circuits, its athletes are questioning whether they'll reap any rewards from this partnership - or even, whether it could "kill" the sport altogether.Stapley, who spoke to BBC Sport from a training camp in Thailand, was having dinner with friends when his phone started pinging with news of the proposals and reaction to them."I was like, hold on a minute, what's this?", said Stapley."We don't even get an early notification, we found out on Instagram".The post read, external: 'Hyrox x World Triathlon are officially introducing 'Hybrid Racing' as a new discipline within the World Triathlon family.'Sophie Evans - who won gold as part of England's Commonwealth Games mixed relay team in Birmingham in 2022 - said she was "surprised" to receive the news like that."I'm not actually against it being part of World Triathlon. It's more the fact we were blindsided, it's just like it's here," she added.Stapley accused World Triathlon of not caring about its athletes because he did not receive any communication from his sport's governing body prior to and after the announcement was made."They have no respect for us," he said. "They don't even contact us like 'hey, do you guys actually care about this, or what do you think?'"In response, a World Triathlon spokesperson told BBC Sport: "The World Triathlon Executive Board approved the partnership. The board includes representatives of the World Triathlon Athletes' Committee elected by their peers."Athlete representatives are involved in every executive board discussion, and their voice is always heard."The announcement was communicated through the same procedures followed for all World Triathlon releases."World Triathlon says the partnership is designed to "benefit the entire World Triathlon movement",, external with new opportunities to engage athletes and audiences, and a stronger platform to grow triathlon and multisport from grassroots to elite level.The question for athletes is, how?European champion Roksana Slupek, of Poland, said she was "not against the idea", but wanted more information."What's the benefit for us, for triathlon? It's nothing against Hyrox," said Slupek.However, Stapley called the move an "attack on our whole existence" and is concerned that World Triathlon could direct attention and resources towards Hyrox's Olympic ambition - at the expense of his own sport."How does Hyrox grow triathlon? If anything they've killed triathlon," he said, while also suggesting brands would rather get in early with Hyrox athletes before they potentially appear at an Olympics."Sponsorships have reduced because there's no visibility on TV, you have to pay to watch us."We are triathletes that do the short distance, which is the Olympic distance, and we've trained all our lives for it."There's no swimming, there's no biking, it's indoors. [Hyrox] has got nothing to do [with triathlon]"."It seems like our sport's gone, 'no worries, come along, use our structure, use our access to the International Olympic Committee, and perhaps take our space'."We've got an opportunity to win medals in Los Angeles [at the 2028 Olympics], but will we have it further down the track?"Evans said that while triathlon was an "established" Olympic sport, that has provided high quality racing since its introduction to the Games 26 years ago, this new partnership has introduced a "level of uncertainty"."A lot of the resistance has come from athletes, because you don't know," she added.A World Triathlon spokesperson told BBC Sport, it is continuing to "increase its focus and involvement in the Olympic and Paralympic families" and that it is in the "planning phase" for Brisbane 2032, adding that "triathlon is, and will remain, at the heart of everything we do".BBC Sport approached Hyrox for comment, but they referred us to the statements made by World Triathlon.Sam Dickinson - who won an Olympic triathlon bronze in Paris as part Team GB's relay quartet - can see why the move makes sense but wants more clarity."It's trying to get people active not from an elite side but from a participation side," Dickinson told BBC Sport."So in that sense it does make sense that as a multi-sport it comes under the World Triathlon umbrella."But it's early days, we don't have any of the bread and butter of exactly what's going on."And there lies the crux of the problem - the lack of clarity has fuelled speculation about what the future holds.World Triathlon does have other disciplines in its remit, such as Aquathlon and duathlon.BBC Sport has been told that 'Fitness Racing' was first included as a discipline in the World Triathlon Constitution in October 2025, a move supported by the majority of the governing body's National Federations.A World Triathlon spokesperson added that the partnership provides opportunities to 'reach new audiences' through collaborating with global partners.Founded in 2017, Hyrox's popularity has continued to grow rapidly. A total of 1.5m athletes took part during the 2025/26 season - up from 650,000 the year before - with participation projected to surpass 2m in the current season.British Triathlon, one of World Triathlon's national federations, told BBC Sport it recognises "World Triathlon's work to grow, develop and strengthen the sport of triathlon, multi-sport and its community", but is waiting to hear the "full operational, governance and commercial framework" for the partnership.

schema.headline: Could Hyrox's Olympic ambition spell the end for triathlon?

title: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic night
description: Figure caption, Watch: The key moments from the US midterm electionsByNorth America correspondentUpdated 8 hours agoDemocrats have torn up Donald Trum
body: Figure caption, Watch: The key moments from the US midterm electionsByNorth America correspondentUpdated 8 hours agoDemocrats have torn up Donald Trump's political map on a night that will send shockwaves through American politics for years to come.With a string of major Senate victories in states that have been reliably Republican for decades - and in Kansas's case, nearly a century - a blue tidal wave crashed across the nation, sweeping Republicans out of power.Halfway through President Donald Trump's second term, the Democrats now have decisive control of the House of Representatives and have wrested a majority back in the Senate. They will be able to frustrate Trump's agenda, and launch investigations into his administration. A historic third impeachment attempt could also be on the cards.Few imagined such an outcome was possible in the months after Trump returned to the White House with unified Republican control of Congress in January 2025. As the public mood turned against him and his party, Democrats had hopes of retaking the House.But they contemplated a Senate map that appeared unfriendly, populated by states Trump had won comfortably just two years ago.Instead, Democrats rewrote the political equations with victories in Texas, Maine, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and North and South Carolina.In comments to the BBC's US partner CBS, Trump pledged to strike deals with congressional Democrats, adding that he didn't want to have to spend his final two years in office rejecting their legislation.He somewhat undermined that sentiment later, posting a picture to Truth Social of his trademark red baseball hat with the word "veto" emblazoned on it.The president went on to note that his name wasn't on the ballot this year, but if it had been Republicans would have won a decisive victory. Trump had helped elevate many of those Republican candidates, however, and had urged voters to pretend he was up for re-election.LIVE: Follow latest updatesREACTION: Trump accepts Democrats did a 'good job' in electionTHE BIG MOMENTS: Ecstatic scenes that greeted key resultsGUIDE: What are the US midterms?In the Senate, Democrats flipped at least six seats, comfortably securing a majority.Adam Hamilton won in Kansas - a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate almost 100 years ago during the Great Depression.James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas' Senate race, ending a 38-year Democratic losing streak in statewide elections there.In South Carolina, Annie Andrews beat Darline Graham, who had been appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham. Few analysts had that seat in play even a few months ago.Five-term Republican Susan Collins conceded Maine's Senate election to Democrat Troy Jackson.Paralympian Josh Turek flipped the Iowa Senate seat held by retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst. Democrats also wrested from Republicans a Senate seat in Ohio, with Sherrod Brown's comeback victory over Jon Husted.Meanwhile, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has beaten Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's bitterly fought Senate race.Nor was that the end of the electoral carnage for Republicans. Ruby-red Texas witnessed another seismic result in the governor's race.Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Republican Greg Abbott, who was earlier this year seen as the prohibitive favourite.Democrats also took governors' races in Iowa, Ohio and Georgia, which made history by electing the first black woman to such a post.Meanwhile, the party has won a House majority for the first time since 2022.They are projected to win 245 House seats and the Republicans 166 seats.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Democrats celebrate in Maine where the party won a crucial Senate raceA look at the key races offers plenty of reasons why.Democrats flipped House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Iowa, Kentucky and Colorado, among others. And they were poised to make gains in Virginia and Indiana. Black Democrats in the southern states turned out in record number, helping to carry their party to victory. And Hispanic voters, whose support had helped secure Trump's presidential victory in 2024, swung decisively back to the Democrats.Democrats won all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border. And Hispanic voters helped Democrats hold House seats in Florida that the state's Republicans had sought to flip by redrawing the congressional district lines.In fact, the congressional redistricting battles that had dominated headlines for months last year ended up being a bust for the Republicans. In Texas, they had hoped their line-drawing would net five new seats for their party. But on Tuesday they may end up losing one seat.If there is a silver lining for conservatives, Florida as a whole still appears to tilt to the right.Republican Senator Ashley Moody narrowly won re-election, as did congressman Byron Donalds, who was elected the Sunshine State's first black governor. And embattled Republicans were able to hold governorships in Vermont and New Hampshire. But the bright spots were few and far between.Just two years ago, Trump won the presidency with 48% of the vote. He claimed an electoral mandate. He then went about governing like it, pushing sometimes unpopular policies on trade and immigration, and launching an Iran war that is opposed by most of the American public.On Tuesday, voters gave him the kind of stinging rebuke that will not be easily forgotten.Figure caption, BBC asks voters across US what brought them to the polls todayFollow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland on historic night

title: Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly
description: Figure caption, Watch: The key moments from the US midterm electionsByJake LaphamUpdated 3 hours agoThe Democrats have swept to victory in the US midt
body: Figure caption, Watch: The key moments from the US midterm electionsByJake LaphamUpdated 3 hours agoThe Democrats have swept to victory in the US midterm elections, taking control of Congress.While the incumbent president's party generally tends to have a bad night in these elections, the scale of the Republican defeat is being viewed as a resounding rejection of Donald Trump's two years in the White House.From angry voters to an unpopular president, here are five reasons why the Republicans lost so many seats. 1. Soaring cost of livingFrom coast to coast, voters across the US have been grappling with the soaring cost of essentials. That anger was palpable on the ground in key races."Gas prices, grocery prices, everything's going up," one North Carolina voter told the BBC ahead of the elections, adding that she had switched her vote from Republican to Democratic this election.Prices increased by 3.7% in the year to September, driven higher by fuel and energy prices. Average US retail diesel prices in early October were just shy of the record of $6.52 (£4.83) per gallon seen in September, according to government data.Almost eight in 10 voters (79%) said inflation had caused them and their family a severe or moderate hardship in the past year, according to data from voter polls.And more than six in 10 respondents laid the blame for that at the feet of Trump, saying they thought higher than usual prices were because of the president's policies. 2. Unpopular Iran warA major factor in surging prices has been the war with Iran which the US and Israel launched in February.Fuel prices then shot up after Tehran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation, strangling a key artery for the passage of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG).US voters have been paying the price at the petrol pump ever since. The war has proved broadly unpopular with most Americans. For Maga Republicans it also felt like a broken promise in Trump's America First campaign agenda in which he pledged there would be no more wars.Around six in 10 (63%) of those asked in a voter poll said the US made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran.Separately, three-quarters of voters (74%) said the conflict was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.The morning after the election, Trump conceded the war had played a role in the  defeat but insisted in an interview on Fox that he had no choice but to intervene to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon.3. Disciplined message from DemocratsThe scale and breadth of this Democratic wave was made possible by some strong candidates who came across as authentic, especially in traditional Republican heartlands.They stuck to a disciplined message about the cost of living and healthcare access.Former teacher James Talarico and pastor Adam Hamilton also talked about their faith in a way that struck a chord in Texas and Kansas respectively.In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews pulled off a shock upset. A former paediatrician, her focus on health care affordability resonated in a country where many see the system as broken.Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed, who triumphed in Michigan to keep that seat Democratic, made getting "money out of politics, money in your pocket" a key slogan.Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who won re-election in Georgia, made the cost of living and corruption a central message. The 39-year-old's comfortable victory in a state Trump won twice will only fuel rumours of a 2028 presidential run. Even Trump himself praised the Democrats, telling Fox News they "did a good job". Conversely, some Republican candidates like Ken Paxton in Texas were criticised for running poor campaigns that were not focused enough on voters' concerns. Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Abdul El-Sayed speaking to supporters in triumph4. Trump's unpopularity a drag on RepublicansTwo of the issues voters were most unhappy with - rocketing prices and the Iran War - were directly linked to the president.His approval ratings had even fallen among Republican voters, which made some of these states which backed him in 2024 especially vulnerable.He urged voters to imagine he was on the ballot in an effort to galvanise his supporters.Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeatBut after more than a decade as the central figure in American politics, some see these results as evidence that the glitz may be wearing off Trump's brand. Against a backdrop of increasing anger, making himself the focus of the Republican campaign was risky and appears to have backfired.In the months leading up to the vote, polling indicated that many Americans wanted Trump to focus more on their concerns about rocketing prices. In his final campaign speech on Monday in Washington DC, he talked at length about his controversial renovation project of the Reflecting Pool behind him. Figure caption, Watch: 'Democrats did a good job,' Trump says5. Hispanic and black voters shift againTwo years ago a move towards Republicans among some Hispanic and black voters helped Trump secure a decisive win. That seems to have reversed in these midterms. Democrats claimed all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border.Majority-Hispanic counties moved more than 22 percentage points against Republican Senate candidates, compared with the 2024 presidential election, according to a New York Times analysis. The change is more than any other major demographic group in the country, data reporter Jeff Adelson said.The shift comes amid widespread anger at immigration enforcement, with a majority (56%) of Americans saying they have an unfavourable opinion of ICE, according to the Pew Research Center.Counties with a black majority also moved significantly towards Democratic candidates in Senate races.The Senate race is on a knife-edge in Mississippi, which has the largest share of black voters of any US state with around 37%.If Scott Colom can win, he would become the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Mississippi since 1982.

schema.headline: Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly

title: 'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
description: Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election resultsByDaniel BushWashington correspondentInside the Republican Party, initial shock
body: Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election resultsByDaniel BushWashington correspondentInside the Republican Party, initial shock at the stunning election results on Tuesday night quickly gave way to anger with US President Donald Trump.After Democrats won upset after upset in deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, some Republicans focused their ire on Trump, arguing that his focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost the party control of Congress."It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told the BBC. "This is a disaster of the first magnitude. Nobody saw it coming like this."Most Republicans expected to lose control of the House and were clear-eyed about the challenge of holding onto the Senate in a tough election cycle that favoured the party out of power. But some said in interviews that Trump dragged them down with unpopular policies, a low job approval rating and obsession over construction projects in Washington."It was just one mistake after another," said Gregg Peppin, a Republican strategist in Minnesota. "Clearly, in state after state, people did not like the president's policies."A White House ally said public disapproval with Trump over the Iran war, tariffs and the administration's immigration crackdown created a "perfect storm" in November."There's palpable frustration [within] the party about how this has all played out," the person said, and much of it is directed at Trump. Anger with Trump "is extremely high".FOLLOW LIVE: Election results and analysis of the US midtermsAnthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland Key moments from a night of midterm election firstsFive reasons why Trump did so badlyThe BBC spoke to a dozen party operatives, campaign officials, White House allies and others, many of whom spoke on background to offer a candid assessment of Trump's approach to the midterms.Trump and Republicans had a lot riding on the outcome on Tuesday night. A stronger showing by the president's party - as happened in 2022, when Democrats under then-President Joe Biden lost just nine seats in the House, and gained one in the Senate - would have given Republicans some momentum heading into 2028.But Trump will instead face a motivated Democratic majority in Congress that is eager to investigate the administration, block his judicial nominees and stymie the rest of his agenda. The midterms have ushered in an uncertain new phase in Trump's second term and may force Republicans to start grappling with their post-Trump future.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The result amounted to a rejection of Trump, one top Republican lobbyist said"I don't think his influence is slipping," said Steve Scheffler, the Republican National Committeeman in Iowa, speaking on the eve of the election. Still, he said, when it came to the midterms, "there were things you wish he said differently".Trump was silent for much of the night before posting a message on Truth Social after the House and Senate were called for Democrats."I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote.He said in later interviews with the New York Times and Fox News that he would accept the election results. Trump told Fox he was a "little bit surprised" by the election results, but noted that the president's party typically fared poorly in midterm elections.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Republican Senator Jon Husted at an election event in Ohio, where the Senate seat flipped in favour of Democrat Sherrod BrownSince 1934, the party in the White House has only gained seats in three midterm elections. While the Democratic gains in 2026 did not set a record, the party did win dozens of House races, state governor contests and Senate seats, including in states where the party had not been competitive for decades.Before Tuesday, Democrats had not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, and had not won a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. The party also notched surprise upsets in other reliably red states like South Carolina that were thought to be safe seats for Republicans just weeks before Election Day.Trump and Vice-President JD Vance held dozens of campaign rallies in the run-up to the midterms. The principal Trump-aligned Super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent hundreds of millions backing Republican candidates.Trump allies said it was unfair to hold him responsible for the party's election losses. They pointed to the history of midterm elections, and said the party was saddled with weak Republican candidates in battleground states like Georgia, Michigan and Texas.Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, ran "the worst Senate campaign in the country from either side of the aisle," said another Texas Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. "If Ken's campaign knocked on 100,000 doors I'd be shocked," the source said. The person added that Paxton's victorious Democratic opponent, James Talarico, ran "a really good and smart campaign."Others defended Trump's autumn campaign schedule, noting that he had to balance his day job of running the country with midterm travel."He's the president. He's not going to spend his time campaigning 24/7," said Krish Mathrani, the Michigan Republican Party's youth chair. Mathrani said Trump's campaign rallies helped drive up enthusiasm among Republican voters. "President Trump is a turnout machine," he said.That's true in presidential elections. But Trump's vaunted turnout operation has failed to deliver in elections when he's not on the ballot, and 2026 proved no different.Voters rejected Trump's argument that the economy was better on his watch and that he was achieving his aims in the war with Iran. The effort by Trump to portray Democrats as extreme socialists also fell flat, as voters handed victories to moderates like Roy Cooper in North Carolina."That just didn't work with Cooper," said a Cooper campaign official. "Trying to tag him as some socialist liberal, that wasn't going to fly."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Republican supporters at a watch party in Iowa, where Democrat candidate Josh Turek won a Senate seat Trump often seemed disinterested in the midterms over the summer, the period of time when Republicans in Congress shifted their focus to the election. Trump was consumed by the war with Iran abroad and his construction overhaul of Washington at home. The projects included the under-construction ballroom and a helipad on the South Lawn of the White House, renovations to a local golf course, a proposed memorial arch near Arlington Cemetery and renovations to the Kennedy Center.Events like a UFC match at the White House on Trump's 80th birthday in June created the impression that the president was more interested in feting himself than winning the midterms, several sources said. Trump also repeatedly downplayed the rising costs of gas and often cast the affordability issue as a Democratic hoax.Trump turned his full attention to the election in September at the Republican Party's midterm convention. The event was a gamble: Republicans hadn't held a midterm convention in decades, and it was an open question whether voters would tune in.Trump dominated the convention in Dallas, frustrating Republicans who told the BBC they wanted to highlight the party's midterm candidates. In his rambling keynote speech, Trump pledged to give $5,000 (£3,700) to anyone who voted for Republicans and raised eyebrows with an endorsement of Paxton which included a lengthy criticism of the candidate's lack of charisma and physical appearance."Obviously, that's never helpful," Robin Armstrong, Texas' Republican National Committeeman, said of Trump's critique of Paxton. "You're not going to stop what President Trump says. We just have to kind of live with that."The convention failed to attract a large television audience, and Democrats were quick to call it a failure. "It backfired for Republicans because nobody paid any attention to it," said Terri Burke, the Texas Democratic Party's executive director.Trump's penchant for straying off-message continued when he hit the campaign trail in the final weeks before Election Day. He made headlines for praising Ohio Republican Senator John Husted's physique, and drew criticism for calling Abdul El-Sayed a "jihadist" in the Michigan Senate race.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mike Rogers in Michigan was among the other losing candidates - having been beaten to a Senate seat by Democrat Abdul El-SayedAs Trump criss-crossed the country stumping for Republican candidates, the White House contended with controversies in Washington. Katie Zacharia was ousted after just five days as White House press secretary, and Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as the US ambassador to Greece after reports surfaced that she asked a donor to pay her credit card debt.Trump also faced a backlash in October for striking a deal to buy Russian diesel. The agreement, which blindsided members of Congress and drew condemnation from some Republicans, came just weeks after Trump signed a sanctions bill aimed at cutting off Russian oil and gas revenue.Democrats used the deal and other scandals swirling around the White House to make the case for retaking control of Congress. The messaging resonated in the end, as Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress in convincing fashion.A second White House ally said that the president's political aides projected optimism until the final days of the election, even as it became clear the party was headed to defeat.Now, as Republicans take stock of the loss, several said they were ready to look ahead to the 2028 election."Whether that's JD Vance, or Macro Rubio, or Ted Cruz, we've got a pretty big bench," said Scheffler, the state's RNC member. "It'll be a wide open race."Peppin, the Republican strategist, said the midterms results demonstrated the party needed a new direction. "I sincerely hope that we've turned the page from the Trump era, and that we'll have new players, new issues and a new focus moving forward."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton was defeated by Democrat James Talarico in Texas

schema.headline: 'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat

title: Government needs to act faster on grooming gang inquiry, says survivor
description: Image caption, Holly says survivors are still waiting for meaningful progress on the inquiry BySarah McMullan and Marina ForceBBC Scotland NewsUpdated
body: Image caption, Holly says survivors are still waiting for meaningful progress on the inquiry BySarah McMullan and Marina ForceBBC Scotland NewsUpdated 5 hours agoA survivor of grooming gang abuse has accused the Scottish government of taking too long to deliver the public inquiry it promised "at pace" almost nine months ago.Holly Alex, 36, went into care at the age of 14 after her stepfather went to prison and her relationship with her mother broke down.Holly's social care records, seen by BBC Scotland News, show that staff recorded concerns that she was being "groomed" for sex by "adult Asian men" as a teenager. They also indicate social workers and police knew of the risks she faced.Education Secretary Màiri McAllan said safeguarding children was the government's priority, and the planned statutory inquiry was a core part of this work.Figure caption, 'I'm speaking up  to give grooming survivors courage'The Scottish government ordered a public inquiry into grooming gangs in February following mounting political pressure.Between the ages of 14 and 17, Holly lived in five different children's homes across Edinburgh.Police Scotland has confirmed it was made aware of some reports made by Holly during this time period and an investigation is ongoing.Image source, Holly AlexImage caption, Holly's social care records indicate social workers and police knew of the risks she facedHolly's care records contain repeated references to her going missing from her accommodation before returning intoxicated, with unexplained sums of money. At the same time, professionals described her as "sexually promiscuous" and "flirtatious".Holly said roughly 25 to 50 men were involved in her abuse in a series of flats in Edinburgh and Livingston during her time in care. What initially appeared to be friendship and generosity, soon became exploitation and abuse."At the start, 14-year-old Holly felt this was great," she said. "But then slowly realised these men expected something from you."It was explicitly told to me: 'You basically need to give us something back, because we gave you all this money, drink, cigarettes, food. We need something back.'"For a while, I thought I was clever because I used to manage to escape before anything happened. "But they caught on to that very quickly and my opportunities to leave became far and few between. "And if I tried to leave, I was met with physical violence."Image source, Holly AlexImage caption, Holly was just 14 years old when she was groomed for sex She added: "Sometimes you'd go to a property and there was maybe two people there, sometimes… seven men there. "I was taken to a specific house and when I arrived there were several men and several young girls. "You never knew what you were walking in to."When asked how she feels about her experience now, Holly said: "Younger me would have said 'disgusting', but it's not my fault."The Scottish government announced plans for a public inquiry into group-based child sexual abuse and exploitation in February, with the then Education Secretary Jenny Gilruth pledging to "leave no stone unturned".'Not tied to ethnicity'Almost nine months on, Holly said survivors were still waiting for meaningful progress."I want them to know that survivors have been waiting, some of us for absolute decades," she said."If you say you'll do something at pace, do it at pace. "Don't just pay lip service to it. Some people's lives depend on the truth coming out."Holly also argued that the term "grooming gang" had become weaponised, creating misconceptions about the nature of the abuse and sometimes "twisted to suit certain narratives". "I am in contact with a lot of survivors who are victims of child sexual exploitation, not by Asian perpetrators, by other perpetrators," she said. She said some survivors had told her they feared being excluded from the inquiry because their abusers did not fit a particular ethnic profile."A grooming gang is a group of two or more perpetrators, regardless of ethnicity or race," she said. "I don't tie grooming gangs specifically to an ethnicity."Image source, Scottish Parliament/PAImage caption, Màiri McAllan said the Scottish government was taking action to determine the scale of abuse by grooming gangsEducation Secretary Màiri McAllan said sexual abuse and exploitation were "abhorrent crimes" that left a devastating effect on victims and their families.She said: "Safeguarding children is our utmost priority, and we are taking determined action to establish the extent and scale of this abuse so we can prevent it."The statutory inquiry is a core part of this work, to be chaired by Prof Alexis Jay with the fullest investigatory powers."A national review of group-based child sexual abuse in Scotland, published in September, external, found there is no reliable national picture of the scale of grooming gang offending because of inconsistent data collection and the absence of an agreed definition.The review was also overseen by Prof Jay, who is a child sexual abuse expert.Before evidence can be heard at the inquiry, its terms of reference must be formally agreed. Ministers are expected to provide an update on the inquiry at Holyrood on Thursday.Holly has been invited to take part in the Scottish government's Truth Project pilot, an exercise to listen to survivors, which is running alongside the public inquiry.Then Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced a statutory independent investigation into grooming gangs in England and Wales in June 2025, with its terms of reference published earlier this year.Police Scotland said it was committed to tackling all forms of child sexual exploitation, regardless of the passage of time. A spokesperson added: "We know how difficult it can be to come forward and the needs of survivors are always at the heart of our victim-centred approach."We will continue to work with partners to identify and to protect potential victims, and to tackle child sexual exploitation and grooming."Holly also experienced sexual abuse at a secure unit in Edinburgh.Her evidence played a crucial role in convicting her abuser, carer Gordon Collins.He was sentenced to 10 years in 2016 for indecent behaviour towards Holly and three other young people in his care. The court heard he raped one girl over the course of a year.Amanda Hatton, from City of Edinburgh Council, said: "We want to repeat our apology to Holly - and praise her and others who have bravely come forward to tell their stories."Testimonies like Holly's have already helped us to make significant changes to the service, including the closure of all secure residential accommodation across the city, and we're confident that children and young people in our care are now safer and better supported."Hatton said the council was listening to young people but acknowledged there was more work to be done to "learn lessons from the past"."If and where any criminality is suspected, we will always report this to Police Scotland urgently," she added.If you have been affected by the issues raised in this article, help and support is available via BBC Action Line.
